title: Factories, cities and shared time
summary: Machines do not automatically create factories. Power, equipment, materials, labor and management must be coordinated continuously in one place. The factory changes not only where production occurs but how people organize shared time.

blocks.text: Machines do not automatically create factories. Power, equipment, materials, labor and management must be coordinated continuously in one place. The factory changes not only where production occurs but how people organize shared time.

Households and workshops could follow different rhythms. Concentrated production required starting times, shifts, discipline and output to fit together. Labor time became more precisely arranged. Efficiency and changing labor relations belonged to the same process.

Industrial cities concentrated population, production and pollution, while railways connected increasingly distant places. Faster transport required shared time. Telegraphy moved information ahead of people and goods, changing the conditions for distant decisions.

These facilities should not be listed merely as separate inventions. Together they changed rhythm, distance and dependence. An interruption at one node could affect a wider area, making new maintenance, rules and responsibilities necessary.
